newsitem.title: USA: New guidelines for Alzheimer's disease treatment.
newsitem.headline: New guidelines for Alzheimer's disease treatment.

text.p: Doctors have scant tools to help patients with Alzheimer's disease, but they can still use their prescription pad to keep them off the road.

Issuing guidelines for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia in the elderly, the American Psychiatric Association said that formally writing out a "Do Not Drive" prescription, instead of just making the recommendation aloud, could have a stronger message.
It could also "lend moral authority and support" to family members trying to keep a demented patient away from the steering wheel.

The association also endorsed the recommendation, released last week in the New England Journal of Medicine, that people with moderate impairment because of Alzheimer's take vitamin E to slow down mental deterioration. Taking the vitamin is not a cure for Alzheimer's but the study suggested it made the disease more gradual.
The guidelines, being published on Thursday in the American Journal of Psychiatry, are the eighth in a series of practice guidelines for mental illness and substance abuse disorders.
The guidelines help define dementia, and help doctors distinguish it from other disorders that can cause similar symptoms, including drug interactions or depression.

A hallmark sign of dementia is memory problems. But the patient may also have trouble using or understanding words, handling common objects, recognising ordinary objects, and difficulty with thinking abstractly, making plans, or starting and stopping complex behaviour.
Some patients with dementia show inappropriate social behaviour. As they deteriorate, they may experience agitation, or even hallucinations.

According to the Alzheimer's Association, up to 4 million Americans have Alzheimer's disease. The psychiatric association said that between a fourth and half of people over age 85 experience dementia, and Alzheimer's is responsible for at least half of that.
